mainEntity.name: How far in advance should a pub plan its marketing?

mainEntity.name: How much should a pub spend on marketing?

mainEntity.name: How do I build a marketing database for my pub?

Within a year, you will have a database of 500 or more people you can reach directly.

mainEntity.name: Should a pub use paid advertising on social media?

Target people within 5 to 10 miles of your postcode, aged 25 to 65. Boost your best-performing organic posts rather than creating separate ads — the engagement is already proven.

mainEntity.name: Should my pub charge for New Year's Eve entry?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your venue. If you have limited capacity and strong demand, a ticketed event protects you from overcrowding and guarantees revenue. If you rely on walk-in trade and your area is competitive, free entry with a pre-booked drinks package can work better. The key is that every person through the door contributes enough spend to justify the staffing and entertainment costs.

mainEntity.name: How much should a pub charge for a New Year's Eve ticket?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most community pubs charge between 10 and 30 pounds per person for a ticketed NYE event, depending on what is included. A ticket that includes a welcome drink, entertainment, and a midnight toast feels like good value at 15 to 25 pounds. If you add a buffet or sit-down meal, 30 to 50 pounds is reasonable. Price based on what customers get, not what it costs you.

mainEntity.name: When should I start promoting my pub New Year's Eve event?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start promoting in late November, at least five to six weeks before the night. Early bird pricing in the first two weeks creates urgency. Use social media, in-venue posters, and your email list. By mid-December most people have made their NYE plans, so the window is short.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert New Year's Eve visitors into regular customers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Collect contact details on the night through a ticket registration, a prize draw entry, or a loyalty card sign-up. Follow up within 48 hours with a thank you message and an invitation to your next event in January. A specific offer like a free drink on their next visit gives people a reason to come back before the end of the month.

mainEntity.name: What entertainment works for a pub New Year's Eve?

acceptedAnswer.text: A DJ or live band is the most popular choice, but it depends on your crowd. For community pubs, a hosted countdown party with music bingo, a quiz, or karaoke often works better than a nightclub vibe. The key is energy and atmosphere. Whatever you choose, book it by October because good acts sell out fast for NYE.

mainEntity.name: What is the national minimum wage for bar staff in 2025?

acceptedAnswer.text: From April 2025 the National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over is 12.21 per hour. For 18 to 20 year olds it is 10.00, and for under 18s it is 7.55. Most experienced bar staff in pubs earn above these minimums to remain competitive, typically 12.50 to 13.50 per hour depending on location and experience.

mainEntity.name: What percentage of revenue should pub wages be?

acceptedAnswer.text: The industry benchmark for total labour costs in a well-run pub is 25 to 30 percent of total revenue. This includes wages, employer National Insurance, pension contributions, holiday pay, and any staff meals or benefits. If you are consistently above 30 percent, your rota needs reviewing or your revenue needs growing.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay overtime or hire another member of staff?

acceptedAnswer.text: As a rule, if you are regularly paying more than 10 hours of overtime per week to one person, it is cheaper to hire a part-timer. Overtime also leads to fatigue, mistakes, and higher staff turnover. Run the numbers including employer NI and pension for a new hire versus the overtime premium, and factor in the risk of burnout.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to pass tips on to staff?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Since October 2024, the Employment (Allocation of Tips) Act requires employers to pass on all tips, gratuities, and service charges to workers in full. You cannot make deductions. You must have a written tips policy and distribute fairly. Keeping tips or using them to top up wages to minimum wage is now illegal.

mainEntity.name: How do I reduce pub labour costs without cutting staff?

acceptedAnswer.text: Focus on rota efficiency first. Match staffing levels to actual trading patterns using EPOS data. Cross-train staff so fewer people can cover more roles. Stagger start and finish times rather than having everyone arrive at the same time. Reduce prep waste that creates unnecessary kitchen hours. And invest in the team you have so turnover drops, because recruitment and training are expensive hidden labour costs.

mainEntity.name: What does wet-led mean in pub terms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wet-led means the pub generates the majority of its revenue from drinks sales, typically 70 percent or more. The term comes from the trade distinction between wet sales (drinks) and dry sales (food). A wet-led pub may serve bar snacks or simple food, but drinks are the primary revenue driver and the business model is built around bar trade.

mainEntity.name: What is a dry-led or food-led pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: A food-led pub, sometimes called dry-led, generates the majority of its revenue from food sales. These venues typically have a full kitchen operation, a dedicated dining area, and food is the primary reason customers visit. Many food-led pubs still do strong drinks trade, but the kitchen drives the business model and the staffing structure.

mainEntity.name: Which is more profitable, wet-led or food-led?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on execution. Wet-led pubs have lower overheads because they need fewer staff and no kitchen operation, and wet GP typically runs at 55 to 65 percent. Food-led pubs have higher revenue potential per head but also higher costs — kitchen staff, ingredients, equipment, and waste. Well-run food operations target 65 to 72 percent GP. The most profitable model is whichever one you execute consistently well.

mainEntity.name: Can a pub switch from wet-led to food-led?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but it is a significant operational change. You need kitchen infrastructure, trained staff, supply chain relationships, and a marketing plan to reposition the pub. It typically takes six to twelve months to establish a food reputation. Many pubs find a phased approach works best — start with a limited menu, prove demand, then expand.

mainEntity.name: What GP should a wet-led pub aim for?

acceptedAnswer.text: A well-managed wet-led pub should target 55 to 65 percent gross profit on drinks, depending on your tie obligations and product mix. Tied pubs buying through a brewery will typically sit at the lower end. Free-of-tie pubs buying on the open market can push toward 65 percent. Premium spirits, cocktails, and wine by the glass have the highest margins.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a pub lease and a pub tenancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: A pub lease is typically 10-25 years, gives you more independence, and often requires you to handle repairs and maintenance. A pub tenancy is shorter (usually 3-5 years), comes with more pubco support but less freedom. Both can include a brewery tie. Choose based on your experience level, financial position, and how much control you want.

mainEntity.name: Can I negotiate my brewery tie without going free of tie?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Start by demonstrating strong performance with increased volumes, reduced wastage, and consistent quality. Then approach your BDM with a clear plan showing how better terms would help you grow further. Evidence-based requests get results. You can also maximise margin on free-of-tie categories like spirits, wines, soft drinks, and coffee.

mainEntity.name: What is the Market Rent Only option and should I use it?

acceptedAnswer.text: MRO lets eligible tied tenants request a free-of-tie lease at market rent. It was introduced by the Pubs Code in 2016 and applies to pub-owning businesses with 500 or more tied pubs. It can work well for operators with strong buying power, but you lose pubco support like marketing funds and cellar equipment. Treat it as a decision, not a default.

mainEntity.name: How much rent should I pay for a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pub rent varies hugely by location, size, and agreement type. As a rough benchmark, rent should typically fall between 8 and 15 percent of your total turnover for a tied pub. For a free-of-tie lease, expect higher rent but lower drink costs. Always get an independent rent assessment before signing or renewing.

mainEntity.name: What happens at the end of my pub lease?

acceptedAnswer.text: At the end of your lease term, you may have a right to renew under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, unless your lease specifically excludes this protection. Your landlord can oppose renewal on limited grounds. If you leave, expect a dilapidations assessment where the landlord inspects the property and may charge you for repairs. Plan for this from day one.

mainEntity.name: What are dilapidations and how do I protect myself?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dilapidations are the costs a landlord claims for repairs and restoration when you leave a pub. They can run into tens of thousands of pounds. Protect yourself by completing a thorough schedule of condition when you move in, photographing everything, maintaining the property throughout your tenancy, and budgeting for end-of-lease costs from the start.

mainEntity.name: Is it better to run a free house or a tied pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither is automatically better. A tied pub typically means higher drink costs but lower rent, plus support from the pubco. A free house gives you buying freedom and potentially better margins, but you pay market rent and handle everything yourself. The right choice depends on your experience, capital, negotiation skills, and local market.

acceptedAnswer.text: Expect to pay between 50 and 150 pounds per month for a cloud-based system, or 1,000 to 5,000 pounds upfront for hardware plus a monthly software subscription. mainEntity.name: Should I choose a cloud-based or server-based EPOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cloud-based is the right choice for almost every pub in 2026. You get automatic updates, remote access to reports, lower upfront costs, and easier multi-site management. Server-based systems still exist but they tie you to on-site hardware and make it harder to access data when you are not in the building.

mainEntity.name: Where is the best place to advertise pub jobs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with your own social media and ask existing staff if they know anyone. Word of mouth consistently produces the best pub hires. For wider reach, use Caterer.com for experienced hospitality candidates, Indeed for volume, and contact local college hospitality departments directly. Avoid paying for premium listings until you have exhausted free channels.

mainEntity.name: How much should I pay bar staff in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: At minimum, pay the National Living Wage, which is reviewed annually. To attract and retain good people, pay above minimum and be transparent about it in your ads. Many pubs now offer 50p to 1 pound above minimum as a starting rate, with a review after three months. Tips, staff meals, and flexible hours also matter — sometimes more than the hourly rate itself.

mainEntity.name: Should I use a trial shift when hiring pub staff?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, always. A trial shift is the single most reliable way to assess whether someone fits your pub. Keep it to three or four hours, pay them for it at the standard rate, and brief your existing team to observe. Watch how they interact with customers, how they handle being busy, and whether they ask questions when unsure.

mainEntity.name: How do I stop pub staff from leaving after a few months?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most pub staff leave because of poor management, not poor pay. The biggest retention drivers are a fair rota published in advance, genuine recognition for good work, opportunities to learn new skills, and a manager who listens. Exit interviews reveal patterns — if three people leave citing the same issue, that issue is your priority.

mainEntity.name: What are the red flags when interviewing for pub jobs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Watch for candidates who badmouth their previous employer, cannot explain gaps in their CV, show no curiosity about your pub, or are vague about availability. In hospitality, reliability matters more than experience. Someone who turns up on time, communicates clearly, and genuinely enjoys being around people will outperform a skilled bartender who calls in sick every other weekend.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to provide a contract for pub staff?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. UK law requires you to provide a written statement of employment particulars on or before the employee's first day. This must include pay, hours, holiday entitlement, notice period, and job title at minimum. Using a template from ACAS is free and protects both you and your staff. Operating without contracts exposes you to tribunal claims and makes it harder to manage performance.

mainEntity.name: Does the Equality Act 2010 apply to pubs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Pubs are classed as service providers under the Equality Act 2010 and must make reasonable adjustments to ensure disabled customers are not placed at a substantial disadvantage. This applies to physical access, communication, and how you deliver your service. Failure to comply can result in legal action and compensation claims.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to install a ramp if my pub has steps?

acceptedAnswer.text: If steps create a barrier for wheelchair users or customers with mobility difficulties, you are required to consider reasonable adjustments. A permanent ramp is ideal, but a portable ramp with a bell or intercom system can be an acceptable alternative for listed buildings or where structural changes are impractical. The key word is reasonable — proportionate to your size and resources.

mainEntity.name: Can I allow dogs in my pub if I serve food?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. There is no UK law preventing dogs in pubs that serve food. The Food Standards Agency guidance states that dogs can be allowed in eating areas at the discretion of the business, provided food hygiene standards are maintained. Most dog friendly pubs allow dogs in the bar area but not the kitchen, and many extend this to dining areas too.

mainEntity.name: What do I need to make my pub family friendly?

acceptedAnswer.text: At minimum you need highchairs, a children's menu or smaller portions, and baby changing facilities. Beyond the basics, consider a small play area or activity packs, a welcoming attitude from staff, and a family-friendly atmosphere during daytime hours. Families spend well when they feel genuinely welcome.

mainEntity.name: How much does it cost to improve pub accessibility?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many improvements cost very little. Large print menus, staff awareness training, and better signage can be done for under 100 pounds. A portable ramp costs 150 to 500 pounds. A full accessible toilet conversion ranges from 3,000 to 8,000 pounds. A hearing loop system costs 200 to 1,000 pounds depending on coverage area. Start with the low-cost changes and build from there.

mainEntity.name: Will allowing dogs put off other customers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Research consistently shows that dog friendly pubs attract more customers than they lose. Around 12 million UK households own a dog, and dog owners actively seek out venues that welcome their pets. Clear zoning, a simple set of house rules, and water bowls by the door signal that you have thought it through. Most non-dog-owning customers are fine with well-behaved dogs in a pub setting.

mainEntity.name: How much does it cost to buy a pub in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the route. A freehold pub can range from 200K to over 1M depending on location and condition. Leasehold premiums typically run 20K to 150K, and tenancy ingoings can be as low as 5K to 30K. On top of any purchase price, budget three to six months of working capital for stock, wages, marketing, and unexpected repairs.

mainEntity.name: Can I buy a pub with no experience?

acceptedAnswer.text: Technically yes, but it is risky. Brewery and pubco tenancies often require evidence of hospitality experience or completion of their training programme. If you are buying freehold with no experience, hire a consultant and consider working in a pub first, even for a few months. The learning curve is steep and mistakes are expensive.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a freehold and leasehold pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Freehold means you own the building and the business outright. You choose your own suppliers and set your own terms. Leasehold means you pay rent and a premium for the right to trade but you do not own the property. Tenancy is similar to leasehold but usually shorter term and often tied to a brewery or pubco for drinks supply.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a personal licence to run a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. At least one person at the premises must hold a personal licence. You obtain this by completing a Level 2 Award for Personal Licence Holders, passing a criminal record check, and applying to your local council. The course takes one day and costs around 150 to 250 pounds.

mainEntity.name: Is buying a pub a good investment in 2025?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be, but it is a lifestyle business not a passive investment. Pubs that succeed have strong operators who are present, adaptable, and focused on their community. If you are looking for hands-off returns, property or shares are simpler. If you want to build something, love hospitality, and are prepared to work hard, a pub can be deeply rewarding.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to complete on a pub purchase?

acceptedAnswer.text: From offer to completion typically takes 8 to 16 weeks for a freehold, and 4 to 12 weeks for a tenancy or lease assignment. Licensing transfers, survey delays, and brewery approvals can all add time. Start the personal licence process early as it runs in parallel.

mainEntity.name: How often do EHO inspections happen?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your current rating and risk category. A premises rated 5 with low risk might not see an inspector for two years. A premises rated 0 to 2, or one flagged as high risk, could be re-inspected within six months. You will not get advance warning of the date — inspections are unannounced.

mainEntity.name: Can I refuse an EHO inspection?

acceptedAnswer.text: Technically an officer needs your consent or a warrant to enter, but refusing or obstructing an inspection is a criminal offence under the Food Safety Act 1990. It also looks terrible and will likely result in a formal follow-up with enforcement action. There is no scenario where refusing helps you.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to get a re-inspection after a bad rating?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can request a re-inspection once you have addressed the issues raised. Most councils allow a re-inspection request after a minimum of three months. You usually pay a fee, typically between 150 and 200 pounds. Only request it when you are genuinely confident the problems are fixed — a second poor score is worse than waiting.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a food hygiene certificate to run a pub kitchen?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no legal requirement for a specific certificate, but you must be able to demonstrate that food handlers are trained in food hygiene. In practice, a Level 2 Award in Food Safety is the industry minimum for kitchen staff, and a Level 3 is expected for the person managing food safety. Inspectors will ask about training records.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I get a food hygiene rating of 0?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rating of 0 means urgent improvement is necessary. The local authority may serve a hygiene improvement notice giving you a deadline to fix specific issues. In serious cases, they can issue a hygiene emergency prohibition notice, which closes your kitchen immediately until the risk is removed. A 0 rating is publicly visible on the Food Standards Agency website and will damage your reputation significantly.

mainEntity.name: Does my food hygiene rating affect my premises licence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not directly, but persistent poor hygiene can lead to enforcement action that creates problems with your licence. If environmental health makes a formal complaint to the licensing authority about your premises, it could trigger a licence review. It also gives ammunition to anyone who wants to object to a licence variation or renewal.

mainEntity.name: Can I hide a bad food hygiene rating?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Your rating is published on the Food Standards Agency website and is publicly searchable. In Wales, displaying your rating sticker is a legal requirement. In England, display is currently voluntary but strongly encouraged, and customers who do not see a sticker will check online. Hiding a bad score does not hide the problem — it just looks like you have something to hide.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a COSHH assessment for pub cleaning products?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Every chemical product used in your pub needs a COSHH data sheet on file and staff must be trained on safe handling. This includes beer line cleaner, glass wash detergent, kitchen degreasers, toilet cleaners, and any cellar treatment chemicals. Keep the data sheets in a folder accessible to all staff, not locked in an office.

mainEntity.name: How do I deal with a noise complaint at my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Take it seriously from the first complaint. Speak to the complainant directly if possible and show willingness to find a solution. Practical steps include checking sound levels with a decibel meter, adjusting speaker placement, setting volume limiters, closing windows and doors during entertainment, and reviewing your finishing times. Keep a written record of every complaint and what you did about it. Your local council environmental health team can advise, and engaging with them proactively is far better than waiting for an enforcement notice.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a licence to put an A-board outside my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most of England you need a pavement licence under the Business and Planning Act 2020, which was made permanent in 2023. The fee is set by your local council and is typically under 100 pounds per year. You must leave at least 1.5 metres of clear pavement for pedestrians. Some councils have blanket bans in conservation areas, so always check before you place your board.

mainEntity.name: How often should I change my pub chalkboard message?

acceptedAnswer.text: At least twice a week. Regulars stop noticing a board that never changes, and passers-by assume a static message means a static pub. Tie your updates to daily specials, upcoming events, or whatever is happening that day. The pubs that get the most social media shares change their boards daily with witty or seasonal messages.

mainEntity.name: What is the best size for a pub A-board?

acceptedAnswer.text: A standard A-board is around 60 by 80 centimetres, which gives you enough space for a headline and a few lines of detail while remaining portable. The text needs to be readable from at least three metres away, so use thick chalk markers and keep your main message to seven words or fewer. Anything smaller gets lost on a busy pavement.

mainEntity.name: Can I use my pub chalkboard on social media?

acceptedAnswer.text: Absolutely, and you should. A well-designed chalkboard is ready-made content. Photograph it at an angle with the pub frontage visible and post it to your socials daily. Some pubs generate thousands of views from a single witty board photo. It costs nothing and reinforces your brand personality to people who may never walk past in person.

mainEntity.name: What should I avoid writing on my pub A-board?

acceptedAnswer.text: Avoid anything that could be seen as discriminatory, offensive, or that makes promises you cannot deliver. Do not advertise prices that are about to change. Avoid clutter and long paragraphs — if someone cannot read and understand your board in three seconds while walking past, it has failed. Also avoid inside jokes that only regulars understand; the A-board exists to attract new customers.

Set a reachable target, say four ales, and reward a completed card with something small like a free half or a branded glass. It quietly turns one pint into several visits.

mainEntity.name: How do I get customers to try cask ale?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lower the risk and make it human. Offer a third-pint or a small taster before they commit, describe each ale in plain English rather than brewery jargon, and have staff recommend one personally. Most people who say they don't like 'real ale' just haven't found the right one yet.

mainEntity.name: How do I keep cask ale in good condition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Keep your cellar at a steady 11–13°C, rotate stock so nothing sits too long, and tap and vent casks in good time so they're ready when you need them. Clean your lines on schedule, check every cask is bright and on form before it goes on, and pull a taster yourself before serving. A great ale poured badly still tastes bad.

mainEntity.name: How do I get my pub on Google Maps?

acceptedAnswer.text: Search for your pub on Google Maps. If it appears, click Claim this business and follow the verification steps. If it does not appear, go to business.google.com, click Add your business, and enter your pub name, address, and category. Google will verify you own the business, usually by sending a postcard with a code to your address. The whole process takes one to two weeks.

mainEntity.name: What categories should I choose for my pub on Google Business Profile?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your primary category should be Pub. Add secondary categories that match what you actually offer, such as Restaurant, Bar, Live Music Venue, or Event Venue. Do not add categories you cannot deliver on. Google uses these to decide which searches show your listing, so accuracy matters more than volume.

mainEntity.name: How do I get my pub into the Google Maps 3-pack?

acceptedAnswer.text: The local 3-pack favours pubs with complete profiles, consistent NAP details across the web, regular photo uploads, frequent Google Posts, strong review scores with recent activity, and a website that matches your listing details. There is no shortcut. Consistency and completeness over time is what moves the needle.

mainEntity.name: How often should I post on Google Business Profile?

acceptedAnswer.text: At least once a week. Posts expire after seven days, so a weekly rhythm keeps your profile active. Share upcoming events, new menu items, seasonal specials, or behind-the-scenes moments. Each post should include a photo, a short description, and a call to action like Book a table or Learn more.

mainEntity.name: Should I respond to negative reviews on Google?

acceptedAnswer.text: Always. Respond within 24 hours, be professional, acknowledge the issue, and offer to resolve it offline. Never argue publicly. Potential customers read your responses as much as the reviews themselves. A thoughtful response to a negative review can actually build more trust than five stars with no replies.

mainEntity.name: Can I add my pub menu to Google Business Profile?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Use the Menu section in your profile to add items with descriptions and prices. You can also upload a PDF or link to your website menu. Keep it updated, especially if prices change seasonally. An outdated menu creates a poor first impression before someone even walks through the door.

mainEntity.name: Do pubs pay VAT on food?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on how the food is served. Hot food and anything eaten on the premises carries 20 percent VAT. Cold takeaway food, such as a sandwich bought to take away, is zero-rated. Most pub food is served hot and eaten in, so the standard 20 percent rate applies to the majority of your food sales.

mainEntity.name: When does a pub need to register for VAT?

acceptedAnswer.text: You must register for VAT when your taxable turnover exceeds 90,000 pounds in any rolling 12-month period, or when you expect it to exceed that threshold in the next 30 days alone. Most pubs pass this threshold quickly. You can also register voluntarily below the threshold if reclaiming input VAT would benefit you.

mainEntity.name: What can a pub reclaim VAT on?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can reclaim VAT on most business purchases including stock from non-tied suppliers, equipment, repairs and maintenance, professional fees, marketing costs, cleaning supplies, and utilities. You cannot reclaim VAT on business entertainment or on items not used for the business. Keep every receipt and invoice.

mainEntity.name: How much does a hospitality accountant cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Expect to pay between 150 and 400 pounds per month for a hospitality-specialist accountant handling your bookkeeping, VAT returns, and annual accounts. Some charge more for payroll. A good one will recover significantly more than their fee through legitimate tax planning and VAT recovery.

mainEntity.name: What is the flat rate VAT scheme for pubs?

acceptedAnswer.text: The flat rate scheme lets you pay a fixed percentage of gross turnover to HMRC instead of calculating the difference between output and input VAT. For pubs the flat rate is typically 6.5 percent. It simplifies admin but you cannot reclaim input VAT on most purchases, so it only suits pubs with low input costs.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to use Making Tax Digital for my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. All VAT-registered businesses must keep digital records and submit VAT returns through Making Tax Digital compatible software. From April 2026 this extends to income tax self-assessment for sole traders and landlords earning over 50,000 pounds. Speak to your accountant about getting compliant.

jsonld.description: Cellar Management: How to Keep Your Beer Perfect and Your Waste Low You could have the best pub in the country — great food, brilliant staff, a cracking quiz...

mainEntity.name: What temperature should a pub cellar be?

acceptedAnswer.text: A pub cellar should be maintained at 11 to 13 degrees Celsius for cask ale. Keg products need to be served colder, typically 3 to 5 degrees, which is handled by the cooling system on the font rather than the cellar temperature itself. If your cellar regularly exceeds 14 degrees, cask ale will condition too fast, go cloudy, and pour with excessive fobbing.

mainEntity.name: How often should beer lines be cleaned in a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Beer lines should be cleaned every seven days without exception. This is the industry standard recommended by the BII and all major breweries. Neglecting line cleaning leads to yeast build-up, off-flavours, and increased wastage from fobbing. A weekly clean takes roughly 30 to 45 minutes for a typical pub cellar and should be logged in a cleaning schedule.

mainEntity.name: What is an acceptable level of beer wastage in a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Industry benchmarks suggest total beer wastage should be between 2 and 3 percent of total volume. This includes ullage from cask conditioning, line cleaning waste, and operational spillage. If your wastage regularly exceeds 4 percent, there is almost certainly a cellar management, line cleaning, or stock rotation problem that needs investigating.

mainEntity.name: What does FIFO mean in pub stock management?

acceptedAnswer.text: FIFO stands for first in, first out. It means the oldest stock is always used before newer deliveries. In a pub cellar, this means placing new casks and kegs behind existing stock so the oldest product is connected and served first. FIFO prevents beer going out of date, reduces ullage, and ensures consistent quality for customers.

mainEntity.name: How do I track ullage and wastage in my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Create a simple ullage log in your cellar. Every time a cask is returned part-full, a keg blows mid-service, or beer is wasted during line cleaning, record the product, volume, date, and reason. Review this log weekly alongside your stock take figures. Patterns in wastage — such as consistently high ullage on a slow-selling cask ale — tell you exactly where to make changes.

mainEntity.name: When should I start promoting Christmas bookings at my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: September is the sweet spot. Corporate bookers and large groups start planning Christmas events in September and October. If you wait until November, the organised groups have already booked elsewhere. Launch your Christmas menu and packages by mid-September and push hard through October.

mainEntity.name: How much deposit should I take for pub Christmas bookings?

acceptedAnswer.text: Take a non-refundable deposit of 10 to 15 pounds per head at the time of booking. For larger groups of 15 or more, consider requiring full pre-payment two weeks before the event. Make your cancellation policy crystal clear on every booking confirmation. This protects you from no-shows that can cost hundreds in wasted food prep.

mainEntity.name: Should I offer a set Christmas menu or a la carte?

acceptedAnswer.text: Offer set menus at two or three price points. Set menus give you predictable margins, easier kitchen prep, faster service, and less waste. You can offer a premium tier with extras like prosecco on arrival or a cheese board to finish. Keep one or two dietary alternatives available but do not run your full menu alongside the Christmas packages.

mainEntity.name: What entertainment works best for pub Christmas parties?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Christmas pub quiz is the easiest win because it fills a midweek slot and needs minimal setup. Live acoustic music works well for Friday and Saturday parties. For larger groups, consider a DJ for the last hour. The key is matching the entertainment to the group size and the night of the week. Do not overspend on entertainment for a Tuesday booking of 12 people.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert December visitors into January regulars?

acceptedAnswer.text: Collect contact details from every Christmas booking. Hand out a January offer card with the bill, something like 20 percent off food in January or a free drink with any main course. Add everyone to your email list and send a New Year message with your January events calendar. The pubs that treat December as a database-building exercise win all year round.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a music licence just to play the radio in my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Any public performance of music requires TheMusicLicence, including playing the radio, streaming from Spotify or Apple Music, or having a TV showing content with music. The only exception is if you are playing music in a private area where no customers or staff can hear it.

mainEntity.name: How much does TheMusicLicence cost for a small pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a typical small pub with a floor area of around 100 square metres, TheMusicLicence for background music costs roughly 500 to 800 pounds per year. The exact fee depends on your rateable value or floor area, your opening hours, and whether you also use music for events, DJs, or live performances.

mainEntity.name: Does TheMusicLicence cover live music and karaoke?

acceptedAnswer.text: TheMusicLicence covers the right to play or perform copyrighted music in any format, including background music, DJ sets, live performances, and karaoke. However, if you are hosting live music you may also need to check your premises licence conditions for entertainment licensing, which is a separate legal requirement.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I play music without a licence?

acceptedAnswer.text: PRS for Music and PPL actively enforce licensing. If caught, you will receive a demand for backdated fees and potentially face court action. Fines can run into thousands of pounds, plus legal costs. It is significantly cheaper to get the licence than to risk enforcement.

mainEntity.name: Is Spotify or Apple Music enough to play music in my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A personal Spotify or Apple Music subscription is licensed for private use only. Playing it in a commercial venue like a pub requires TheMusicLicence on top of your streaming subscription. Some providers offer commercial streaming plans, but these do not replace TheMusicLicence either.

mainEntity.name: Can I play royalty-free music to avoid needing a licence?

acceptedAnswer.text: In theory yes, but it is risky. Every track must genuinely be royalty-free and not registered with PRS or PPL. If even one track in your playlist is registered, you are in breach. Most landlords find it simpler and safer to get TheMusicLicence and play whatever they want.

mainEntity.name: How much does pub insurance cost per year?

acceptedAnswer.text: A small community pub typically pays 2,000 to 5,000 pounds per year for a combined policy covering public liability, employers liability, buildings, contents, and business interruption. Larger food-led venues with higher turnover and more staff can pay 5,000 to 10,000 pounds or more. The biggest factors are your turnover, number of employees, building value, and claims history.

mainEntity.name: Is public liability insurance a legal requirement for pubs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Public liability insurance is not technically a legal requirement, but it is a practical necessity. Without it, a single slip-and-fall claim could bankrupt your business. Most brewery and pubco tenancy agreements require it as a condition of your lease, typically with a minimum of 5 million pounds cover. No sensible licensee should trade without it.

mainEntity.name: Is employers liability insurance legally required for pubs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. If you employ anyone, even part-time bar staff or a casual glass collector, you are legally required to have employers liability insurance of at least 5 million pounds. Most policies provide 10 million pounds as standard. Failing to have it is a criminal offence with fines of up to 2,500 pounds per day you are uninsured.

mainEntity.name: Does pub insurance cover live music and events?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard public liability policies usually cover regular pub activities including live music, quiz nights, and other events, but check the small print. Some policies exclude certain event types, outdoor events, bouncy castles, or activities involving fire. If you run large-scale events or anything unusual, tell your insurer in advance. Undisclosed activities can void your cover.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between buildings and contents insurance for a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Buildings insurance covers the physical structure including walls, roof, floors, fixtures, and permanent fittings. Contents insurance covers everything inside that you could take with you if you moved, such as furniture, glassware, stock, kitchen equipment, and electronics. If you are a tenant, your landlord or pubco usually insures the building, but you need contents cover for your own assets.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pub insurance if I have had a claim refused or a policy cancelled?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but it will be harder and more expensive. Specialist licensed trade brokers are your best route because they work with insurers who understand pubs. Be upfront about your claims history. Lying or omitting information will invalidate any future claim, which is far worse than paying a higher premium.

mainEntity.name: What should I say to my landlord if I can't pay the rent on time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Contact them before the payment is due, not after. Present your current trading figures, a realistic forecast, and a proposed repayment plan. Landlords prefer tenants who communicate openly and show a path to recovery over tenants who go silent and force them to chase.

mainEntity.name: Can I negotiate better terms with my drinks supplier?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — suppliers would rather adjust terms than lose an account. Ask for extended payment windows, volume-based discounts, or promotional support. Come with data showing your order history and future projections. Even small concessions on payment terms can ease weekly cash flow significantly.

mainEntity.name: Should I get professional help with pub financial negotiations?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the amounts are significant or you are facing legal action, yes. The BII offers member support, and there are specialist hospitality accountants who understand pub leases and supplier contracts. For smaller negotiations, a clear data pack and an honest conversation often achieve the same result.

mainEntity.name: How much does a basic pub toilet refurbishment cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A budget refresh covering paint, lighting, mirrors, and hand drying typically costs between 500 and 1,500 pounds per room depending on size and condition. A full strip-out with new cubicles, flooring, and plumbing runs 5,000 to 15,000 pounds or more. Start with the cosmetic upgrades first because they deliver the biggest perception shift for the lowest spend.

mainEntity.name: What is the single most impactful upgrade for pub toilets?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lighting. Swapping flickering fluorescent tubes for warm LED panels or spotlights changes the entire feel of the room instantly. It costs under 200 pounds, takes an afternoon to fit, and makes everything else look better — including the paint, the mirrors, and the cleanliness.

mainEntity.name: Hand dryers or paper towels in a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most pubs, a decent automatic hand dryer wins on long-term cost and hygiene. A good unit costs 200 to 500 pounds and lasts years with minimal maintenance. Paper towels create litter, block drains, and need constant restocking. If you do choose towels, use a wall-mounted dispenser and a covered bin, never a basket.

mainEntity.name: How often should pub toilets be deep cleaned?

acceptedAnswer.text: At minimum, a full deep clean once a week with daily spot checks and hourly checks during busy sessions. A signed cleaning log on the back of the door shows customers you take it seriously and gives staff accountability. Most complaints come from the gap between closing and the next lunchtime when nobody checks.

mainEntity.name: Should I refurbish pub toilets myself or hire a contractor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Paint, mirrors, lighting, and accessories are all DIY-friendly if you are reasonably handy. Plumbing, tiling, and cubicle installation are better left to professionals. The cosmetic work is where you get the most impact per pound, so doing it yourself can cut 50 to 70 percent of the cost.

mainEntity.name: What are the best Halloween food ideas for a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Keep it warming, shareable, and high-margin. Loaded nachos badged as 'witches' fingers', chilli served in a hollowed bread bowl, pumpkin soup, and toffee apples or sticky toffee pudding for afters all photograph well and cost pennies to dress up. Put one or two dark cocktails on the bar — a rum punch or a green apple sour with a bit of dry ice — and you lift the average spend without touching your kitchen prep much.

mainEntity.name: What are good Halloween party ideas for adults at a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: A ticketed adult Halloween party night works best: charge a small entry fee, include a drink on arrival, and run a fancy dress competition with a bar tab as the prize so the winner spends it with you. Pair it with a Halloween cocktail menu and a themed quiz, and hold it on the nearest Friday or Saturday rather than midweek so people can actually turn up. Halloween 2026 falls on Saturday 31 October, which makes that weekend an easy one to build around.

mainEntity.name: How far in advance should I promote a pub Halloween event?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start six weeks before, around mid-September. Post a mark-your-calendar on social media, add the event to your Google Business Profile, and open ticket sales or bookings at least three weeks out. A countdown series on social media in the final two weeks builds urgency and fills late seats.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a TEN for a pub bonfire night event?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you are selling alcohol within your existing licensed hours and on your licensed premises, you do not need a Temporary Event Notice. However, if you plan to extend hours, serve alcohol in an unlicensed outdoor area, or host the event off-site, you may need a TEN. Check with your local council at least four weeks in advance.

mainEntity.name: Can a pub legally have a bonfire or fireworks?

acceptedAnswer.text: You need to check with your local council and fire service. Most urban pubs cannot safely host a live bonfire, but a fire pit or chiminea in a beer garden can create the atmosphere. For fireworks, you typically need a licensed display operator and public liability insurance. Many pubs find it easier to partner with a local fireworks display and host the after-party instead.

mainEntity.name: What food should a pub serve for bonfire night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Think warming, shareable, and high-margin. Loaded hot dogs, chilli con carne with jacket potatoes, pulled pork buns, and soup in mugs all work well. Toffee apples, parkin, and sticky toffee pudding are traditional dessert options. A set bonfire menu at a fixed price simplifies kitchen ops and protects your margin.

mainEntity.name: How do I make a pub Halloween event family-friendly during the day?

acceptedAnswer.text: Run a daytime session between midday and three in the afternoon, separate from any adult evening event. Pumpkin carving, a fancy dress parade with small prizes, and a simple treasure hunt around the pub keep children entertained. Serve a kids meal deal alongside your regular menu so parents spend on food and drinks while the children are occupied.

jsonld.description: Running a pub looks simple from the other side of the bar. Pull pints, chat to regulars, lock up at closing time. The reality is that running a pub is one of...
jsonld.keywords: How do I run a pub?, What do I need to know about running a pub?, How to be a good pub landlord?, What are the basics of pub management?, How much does it cost to run a pub?, What qualifications do I need to run a pub?, How do I make my pub profitable?

mainEntity.name: What qualifications do I need to run a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: You need a personal licence, which requires completing an accredited licensing qualification (typically a one-day course costing around 150-250 pounds). Your premises also needs a premises licence. If you serve food, at least one person must hold a Level 2 Food Hygiene certificate. Beyond formal qualifications, practical experience in hospitality, basic financial literacy, and strong people skills are what actually determine success.

mainEntity.name: How much does it cost to run a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Costs vary hugely depending on whether you are a tenant, leaseholder, or freehold owner. A tied tenancy might require 5,000-20,000 pounds upfront with weekly rent of 500-2,000 pounds. A free-of-tie lease could need 50,000-150,000 pounds ingoing. Monthly running costs for a typical community pub include rent, stock, wages, utilities, insurance, and licensing fees. Your biggest ongoing costs will be stock (around 35-40 percent of turnover), wages (20-30 percent), and rent.

mainEntity.name: What gross profit percentage should a pub aim for?

acceptedAnswer.text: A well-run pub should target 60-65 percent GP on wet sales and 65-70 percent on food. At The Anchor, careful menu engineering and portion control grew our food revenue by 98 percent in three months. If your overall GP is below 55 percent, you are losing money on some lines and need to review pricing, supplier deals, and wastage immediately.

mainEntity.name: How do I attract more customers to my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with consistent events run every single week without fail — at The Anchor, that discipline helped grow table bookings by 403 percent. Combine that with active social media (which grew our Google Search visibility by 828 percent), a Google Business Profile that is fully optimised, and genuine community engagement. The biggest mistake is trying everything at once. Pick two or three things, do them well, and build from there.

mainEntity.name: What are the most common mistakes new pub landlords make?

acceptedAnswer.text: The biggest mistakes are underestimating working capital needs, trying to change everything on day one, not tracking GP weekly, hiring friends instead of skilled staff, and competing on price instead of value. Most new licensees also underestimate how physically and emotionally demanding the role is. Get your finances and your support network sorted before you take on a pub.

mainEntity.name: How many hours a week does running a pub take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Honestly, expect 60-80 hours a week in your first year, especially if you are hands-on behind the bar and in the kitchen. As you build a reliable team and put systems in place, you can work towards 50-60 hours. The licensees who burn out are the ones who try to do everything themselves. Delegation and smart use of technology are essential for sustainability.

mainEntity.name: Is running a pub profitable?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be, but margins are tighter than most people expect. A well-run community pub might generate 10-15 percent net profit on turnover. The key levers are GP management, labour efficiency, and driving revenue through events and food. Pubs that treat it as a proper business — tracking numbers weekly, controlling costs, and actively marketing — are far more likely to be profitable than those winging it.

mainEntity.name: What counts as a pop-up event for a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Any short, one-off takeover that gives people a fresh reason to visit: a street-food trader for one night, a guest chef using your kitchen, a makers' market in the garden, or a themed supper club. It runs once or on a set rhythm rather than every day, which is what makes it feel like an occasion.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a Temporary Event Notice for a pop-up?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. If a trader serves food within your normal licensed hours and footprint, you are covered by your existing premises licence. You only need a Temporary Event Notice if you extend your hours or trade outside your licensed area, such as spilling out into a car park. Check your own licence conditions first.

mainEntity.name: How do I find traders or guest chefs for a pop-up?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start local. Message street-food traders you have seen at nearby markets, ask your suppliers who they rate, and post in local hospitality and community Facebook groups. Most independent traders are actively looking for covered, marketed venues with a built-in crowd, which is exactly what your pub offers.

mainEntity.name: How often should I run pop-up events?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pick one format and run it on a predictable rhythm, such as the first Friday of the month, rather than scattering one-offs. Consistency is what turns a pop-up from a gamble into a habit your locals plan around. Monthly is plenty for most pubs while you build the audience.

mainEntity.name: How quickly should I respond to a bad pub review?

acceptedAnswer.text: Within 24 hours is the benchmark. Speed signals that you care and are actively managing the business. A fast, professional response also stops the review sitting unanswered while potential customers read it and form opinions. Set up Google and TripAdvisor notifications on your phone so you never miss one.

mainEntity.name: Should I offer a free meal to someone who left a bad review?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not publicly. A public offer of compensation trains people to complain for freebies and can look desperate. Instead, acknowledge the problem, apologise genuinely, and invite them to contact you directly. If you resolve it privately and they return, they often update the review themselves. The goal is relationship recovery, not bribery.

mainEntity.name: Can I get a fake or unfair review removed?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can flag reviews that violate platform guidelines, such as spam, reviews from people who never visited, or reviews containing hate speech. Google and TripAdvisor both have reporting tools. However, a review being harsh or unfair is not grounds for removal. Your best strategy is a professional response that shows future readers your side of the story, plus generating enough genuine positive reviews that one bad one has minimal impact.

mainEntity.name: How do I get more positive reviews for my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask at the point of delight, not at the point of payment. When someone compliments the food, thanks you for a great quiz night, or tells you they had a lovely evening, that is the moment to say: We would really appreciate a Google review if you have a minute. Table cards with a QR code linking to your review page make it effortless. Aim for two to three new reviews a week, not a sudden burst.

acceptedAnswer.text: A typical community pub turning over 400K to 600K per year can expect owner's profit of 20K to 60K after all costs including rent, wages, stock, and overheads. Higher-turnover food-led pubs can net more, but they also carry higher costs. The range is wide because profit depends on your GP margins, labour control, and how much of your turnover leaks through waste, poor pricing, and unnecessary spend.

mainEntity.name: What is a good gross profit for a pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: For wet sales (drinks), target 60-65% gross profit. For food, target 65-70%. A blended GP across the whole business should sit between 60% and 68% depending on your wet-to-food ratio. If your food GP is below 60%, your menu is costing you money. At The Anchor, tightening food GP through portion control, supplier renegotiation, and menu engineering helped us grow food revenue by 98% in three months.

mainEntity.name: What is the average turnover of a pub in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: Average UK pub turnover varies enormously by type and location. A small wet-led village pub might turn over 150K to 250K. A busy community local doing food and drink could manage 400K to 700K. A large food-led destination pub can exceed 1M. The number that matters more than turnover is what percentage you keep as profit.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate my pub break-even point?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add up all your fixed costs for the year: rent, rates, insurance, utilities, loan repayments, and any salaried staff. Divide that total by your blended gross profit percentage (expressed as a decimal). The result is your break-even turnover. For example, if fixed costs are 150K and your blended GP is 62%, your break-even is 150K divided by 0.62, which equals roughly 242K in annual turnover.

mainEntity.name: What percentage should pub labour costs be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Labour costs should sit between 25% and 30% of turnover for most pubs. Below 25% and you are probably understaffed, which hurts service and trade. Above 30% and wages are eating your profit. Food-led pubs tend to run higher labour costs because of kitchen staff, so aim for the lower end on wet-led and accept the higher end if food is a major revenue stream.

mainEntity.name: Why is my pub not making money?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common reasons are poor gross profit margins on drinks or food, labour costs that are too high relative to turnover, excessive waste and stock shrinkage, underpricing, and failing to track the numbers weekly. Most pubs that struggle are not short of customers — they are short of margin. Start by measuring your GP on drinks and food separately, then work through this guide to find where the leaks are.

mainEntity.name: How much does a premises licence cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: The application fee depends on the rateable value of your premises. For most small to medium pubs the initial fee is between 100 and 635 pounds, with an annual maintenance fee in a similar range. The biggest cost is often the solicitor or licensing consultant you use to prepare the application, which can add 1,000 to 3,000 pounds on top.

mainEntity.name: Can I sell alcohol without a personal licence?

acceptedAnswer.text: You cannot be named as the Designated Premises Supervisor without a personal licence. However, other staff can sell alcohol under the authority of the premises licence as long as there is a named DPS who holds a personal licence. In practice, every pub landlord should have one.

mainEntity.name: How many TENs can I apply for in a year?

acceptedAnswer.text: A single premises can have a maximum of 15 TENs per calendar year, covering no more than 21 days in total. A personal licence holder can give 50 TENs per year, while someone without a personal licence can give only 5. Each TEN can cover an event of up to 499 people for up to 168 hours, which is 7 days.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to get a premises licence?

acceptedAnswer.text: The statutory consultation period is 28 days from the date the application is properly made. If there are no objections, the licence is usually granted shortly after that. If there are representations from responsible authorities or local residents, a licensing committee hearing is scheduled, which can add 4 to 8 weeks. Budget 2 to 3 months total.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I run an event without a TEN?

acceptedAnswer.text: Selling alcohol or providing regulated entertainment without the correct authorisation is a criminal offence under the Licensing Act 2003. You could face a fine of up to 20,000 pounds or six months in prison. Your premises licence could also be reviewed and revoked. It is never worth the risk.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a licence for live music in my pub?

acceptedAnswer.text: Since the Live Music Act 2012, unamplified live music between 8am and 11pm is exempt from licensing for any venue. Amplified live music is exempt for audiences of up to 500 people between 8am and 11pm if your premises already has a premises licence authorising the sale of alcohol. If you want music after 11pm or for larger audiences, you need it on your premises licence or covered by a TEN.

mainEntity.name: Can my premises licence be revoked?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Any responsible authority or any person can apply for a review of your premises licence at any time. Common triggers include persistent noise complaints, underage sales, crime and disorder, and public safety concerns. At a review hearing the licensing committee can modify conditions, suspend the licence for up to three months, remove the DPS, or revoke the licence entirely.
